title: Short is enough (Berakhot 34a)
hook: the Talmud points to Moses' five-word prayer: a short prayer is fine

segments.voice: Yesterday, the prayer of the road. Your line was safe on the way. Did you say your sentence at the door? Today, the end of the week, and a prayer of five words. Day six hundred thirty-seven.

A study hall, long ago. A student is leading the prayer, and he goes on. And on. Every line stretched, every word drawn out. The other students shift on their benches and finally complain to their teacher, Rabbi Eliezer. How long is this going to take? Another day, a different student leads, and he races through it, done almost before he's started. The students complain again. Too short! Rabbi Eliezer has one answer for both, and both answers point to Moses.
screen: `ONE STUDENT GOES ON AND ON.` → `ANOTHER RACES THROUGH.` → `ONE TEACHER, TWO ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: The story is in the Talmud, Berakhot 34a. To the complainers about the long prayer, Rabbi Eliezer says: is he taking longer than Moses? Moses lay on his face before God for forty days and forty nights, pleading for the people after the golden calf. To the complainers about the short prayer, he says: is he any shorter than Moses? And he quotes the moment in the book of Numbers when Moses' sister Miriam is struck with a skin disease. Moses cries out: "Heal her now, O God, I beseech Thee." In Hebrew it's five short words: El na, refa na lah. God, please, heal, please, her. That's the whole prayer. No opening praise, no long explanation. Two pleases and a name. And it's enough. After seven days outside the camp, Miriam is brought back in. The lesson Rabbi Eliezer draws isn't that short is better or long is better. It's that both are real prayer. There's a time for forty days on your face, and a time for five words cried out in a hallway. The length doesn't make it count. That's the week's last word on personal prayer, and it ties the week together. We started with the tkhine, prayer at the kitchen stove. Then Rebbe Nachman's own words, the early pious waiting an hour, the dry days, the prayer of the road. Long or short, fixed or free, Hebrew or Yiddish: the tradition makes room for all of it.
screen: `TOO LONG, TOO SHORT.` · `FORTY DAYS ON HIS FACE.` · `EL NA, REFA NA LAH.` · `BOTH ARE REAL PRAYER.` · then, large: `SHORT IS ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a short prayer for someone. Think of one person who's struggling right now: ill, worried, grieving. Picture their face. If you pray, you can borrow Moses' shape: their name, and please, and the one thing they need. Five words or fewer. If you don't pray, say a five-word wish for them, out loud. Then sit with their face for the rest of the time. You don't need to add more. The bell holds the time.
Short is enough. Moses' five-word prayer for Miriam, El na, refa na lah, which the Talmud holds up as proof that a brief prayer is real prayer.

Your line: short is enough. A week of rain and dew, the kitchen tkhine, your own words, waiting an hour, the heart that follows, safe on the way. Today, send one five-word wish to someone who needs it. Day six hundred thirty-seven.

howItsDone: Many Jews add a brief personal prayer for the sick, often naming the person, in the Amidah's blessing for healing or at the Mi Sheberach when the Torah is read; Moses' words for Miriam are often cited as a model.

original.note: Hebrew: God, please, heal her, please (Numbers 12:13).

trapdoor: what you thought: real prayer has to be long.
what it means: the length doesn't make it count; five words cried out are a whole prayer.
what a scholar hears: Berakhot 34a sets Numbers 12:13 against Deuteronomy 9:25's forty days, so both are allowed.
